lesson.title: Slow Start: Probing Bandwidth Quickly
lesson.summary: Explains how TCP's slow-start phase uses exponential growth of the congestion window, driven by returning ACKs, to quickly discover usable network capacity after a connection begins.
lesson.body:
You already know that congestion control exists because a sender has no direct way to see how much capacity the path to the receiver can handle, and sending too fast causes queues to overflow and packets to be dropped. Slow start is the specific strategy TCP uses to answer the very first version of that problem: when a connection is brand new, the sender knows nothing about the path at all, so how should it choose its initial sending rate?

The answer is to start cautiously but grow fast. TCP begins with a small congestion window, commonly around ten segments, meaning the sender can have that many segments in flight before waiting for acknowledgment. Instead of guessing a large number and risking an immediate overload, the sender begins low and increases the window as evidence accumulates that the network can handle more. That evidence comes in the form of ACKs: every time an ACK arrives confirming a segment was delivered, the sender increases its congestion window by roughly one segment's worth. Because a full window of segments generates a full window of ACKs within about one round-trip time, this simple rule has a powerful compounding effect, the window effectively doubles every RTT rather than growing by a fixed amount.

Trace through the numbers to see why this matters. Suppose the initial window is 10 segments. In the first RTT, the sender transmits those 10 segments and receives 10 ACKs, each bumping the window up by one, so the window becomes 20. In the second RTT, it sends 20 segments, gets 20 ACKs, and the window becomes 40. By the fourth RTT it's near 160. This is exponential growth, which is dramatically faster than increasing by a constant amount each round-trip. The name "slow start" refers only to the modest starting point, not to the pace of growth once underway, within just a few round-trips the window can be many times its original size.

This exponential ramp-up doesn't continue forever. Slow start ends when one of two things happens. First, the congestion window may reach a value called the slow-start threshold, a limit the connection maintains based on past experience with this path; once the window crosses that threshold, TCP shifts into a more cautious, linear growth phase to fine-tune around the network's actual capacity. Second, and more commonly early in a connection's life, slow start ends because a packet loss is detected, which is the network's way of signaling that the sender has finally pushed past what the path can absorb. When that happens, the sender treats the point just before the loss as a signal about the path's real capacity, lowers its threshold accordingly, and restarts the process cautiously.

The reason this exponential-then-brake pattern makes sense is efficiency under uncertainty: doubling each RTT lets the sender discover available bandwidth in a logarithmic number of round-trips rather than a linear one, so a connection reaches a reasonable operating point quickly instead of creeping upward for a long time. At the same time, because the growth is still window-based and paced by real ACKs rather than sent all at once, the sender never floods the network faster than packets are actually being delivered, which keeps the aggressive ramp-up from being reckless.
